Título: La importancia de los factores climáticos en la decisión de instalar paneles fotovoltaicos

Greenpeace aboga por la utilización de energías renovables a nivel mundial. Sin embargo, la decisión de instalar paneles fotovoltaicos para autoconsumo está sujeta a los factores climáticos de una región. La producción de energía solar está directamente afectada por el clima, y ​​es vital evaluar el impacto de las variaciones climáticas en la producción de energía antes de instalar un sistema fotovoltaico.

Uno de los factores críticos a evaluar es la cantidad de luz solar que reciben los paneles a lo largo del día. Es imperativo asegurarse de que la región tenga suficiente luz solar durante todo el año, particularmente en áreas con inviernos más largos. La falta de luz solar afecta drásticamente la producción de energía. Además, factores como la cobertura de nubes, la humedad, la precipitación y la temperatura promedio afectan la cantidad de energía solar que los paneles pueden absorber. Por lo tanto, es necesaria una evaluación exhaustiva de estos factores para determinar la viabilidad de instalar un sistema de paneles solares.

La lluvia y las precipitaciones son esenciales para el funcionamiento óptimo de los paneles solares, ya que ayudan a refrescarlos. Además, las temperaturas más bajas mejoran la eficiencia de los paneles. Sin embargo, las temperaturas más altas provocan variaciones significativas en la productividad, mientras que las regiones propensas a tormentas pueden dañar los paneles y, por lo tanto, reducir su eficacia. Así, las condiciones climáticas juegan un papel crucial a la hora de decidir la instalación de un sistema fotovoltaico para autoconsumo.

Es crucial buscar la evaluación de un experto antes de instalar un sistema de energía solar. La evaluación de un experto ayudaría a determinar la viabilidad de la instalación en función de los factores climáticos de la región. Al evaluar todos los factores climáticos, se puede tomar una decisión informada sobre la instalación de un sistema fotovoltaico para autoconsumo.

Please write code for this homework that runs bare metal program on raspi 3

Lab 1: Hello World
Introduction
In Lab 1, you will practice bare metal programming by implementing a simple shell. You need to set up mini UART, and let your host and rpi3 can communicate through it.

Goals of this lab
Practice bare metal programming.

Understand how to access rpi3’s peripherals.

Set up mini UART.

Set up mailbox.

Basic Exercises
Basic Exercise 1 - Basic Initialization - 20%
When a program is loaded, it requires,

All it’s data is presented at correct memory address.

The program counter is set to correct memory address.

The bss segment are initialized to 0.

The stack pointer is set to a proper address.

After rpi3 booting, its booloader loads kernel8.img to physical address 0x80000, and start executing the loaded program. If the linker script is correct, the above two requirements are met.

However, both bss segment and stack pointer are not properly initialized. Hence, you need to initialize them at very beginning. Otherwise, it may lead to undefined behaviors.

Todo

Initialize rpi3 after booted by bootloader.

Basic Exercise 2 - Mini UART - 20%
You’ll use UART as a bridge between rpi3 and host computer for all the labs. Rpi3 has 2 different UARTs, mini UART and PL011 UART. In this lab, you need to set up the mini UART.

Todo

Follow UART to set up mini UART.

Basic Exercise 3 - Simple Shell - 20%
After setting up UART, you should implement a simple shell to let rpi3 interact with the host computer. The shell should be able to execute the following commands.

command

Description

help

print all available commands

hello

print Hello World!

Important

There may be some text alignment issue on screen IO, think about \r\n on both input and output.

Todo

Implement a simple shell supporting the listed commands.

../_images/lab1_example1.png
Basic Exercise 4 - Mailbox - 20%
ARM CPU is able to configure peripherals such as clock rate and framebuffer by calling VideoCoreIV(GPU) routines. Mailboxes are the communication bridge between them.

You can refer to Mailbox for more information.

Get the hardware’s information
Get the hardware’s information is the easiest thing could be done by mailbox. Check if you implement mailbox communication correctly by verifying the hardware information’s correctness.

Todo

Get the hardware’s information by mailbox and print them, you should at least print board revision and ARM memory base address and size.

Advanced Exercises
Advanced Exercise 1 - Reboot - 30%
Rpi3 doesn’t originally provide an on board reset button.

You can follow this example code to reset your rpi3.

Important

This snippet of code only works on real rpi3, not on QEMU.

#define PM_PASSWORD 0x5a000000
#define PM_RSTC 0x3F10001c
#define PM_WDOG 0x3F100024

void set(long addr, unsigned int value) {
    volatile unsigned int* point = (unsigned int*)addr;
    *point = value;
}

void reset(int tick) {                 // reboot after watchdog timer expire
    set(PM_RSTC, PM_PASSWORD | 0x20);  // full reset
    set(PM_WDOG, PM_PASSWORD | tick);  // number of watchdog tick
}

void cancel_reset() {
    set(PM_RSTC, PM_PASSWORD | 0);  // full reset
    set(PM_WDOG, PM_PASSWORD | 0);  // number of watchdog tick
}

conclusion might be wrong, it might be right, but his reasoning is

is thinking, and what machines do is not. His justification gives
exceptionalism a bad name!  He arrogantly defines all that humans do
as thinking and he denies that machines can think because they are
machines. That is what he says in his article again and again. And he
states this prejudice as his conclusion, as if he got there by reasoning.

        Here’s an example. Suppose you are holding an apple in your

        “The apple falls.” That is a description. A prediction
        might have been the statement “The apple will fall if I open
        my hand.” Both are valuable, and both can be correct. But an
        explanation is something more: It includes not only descriptions
        and predictions but also counterfactual conjectures like “Any
        such object would fall,” plus the additional clause “because
        of the force of gravity” or “because of the curvature of
        space-time” or whatever. That is a causal explanation: “The
        apple would not have fallen but for the force of gravity.”
        That is thinking.

Yes, that is thinking. Chomsky thinks here he is telling us what only
humans do. Task by task
he describes a human ability and then he says, "That is thinking."

all of these tasks also. If Chomsky concludes "that is thinking" then
that must be evidence of thinking for anything which can do those tasks.
According to Chomsky's own argument ChatGPT can think.

What all (but a tiny handful of humans) are doing when they say “The
apple would not have fallen but for the force of gravity” is precisely
what ChatGPT is doing when it too says the same, and it does say the
same. Both humans and ChatGPT are merely merely reciting what they

of gravity. And ChatGPT knows this in the same way as humans, it's
in the training data of humans and AI.  Humans do not work this out,

capabilities in his example.  ChatGPT can do the description of the
apple falling and the prediction that it will fall. It can do what Chomsky
unnecessarily uses technical language for, it can do the "counterfactual
conjecture", it knows that all objects fall!  ChatGPT knows this is
“because of the curvature of space-time”.  ChatGPT knows this
"causal explanation" better than most humans. ChatGPT knows “The
apple would not have fallen but for the force of gravity.” Yes,
and here I agree with Noam Chomsky: He says of the "causal
explanation" that "That is thinking."

UNLESS thinking is defined as something that humans do and ChatGPT
does not.  The only way Chomsky can support his assertion is by defining
"thinking" and "knowing" and "description" and "prediction" and "generalising"
etc etc as being that which are uniquely human capabilities.  Chomsky's argument

predicate that only humans can think. He concludes, after many paragraphs
of delusional obfuscation that thinking is what only humans can do.

How do search algorithms work?Search algorithms are used to find and retrieve information from a collection of data, such as a database or the internet. The most common type of search algorithm is the keyword-based search, which is used by search engines like Google, Bing, and Yahoo.These search engines use web crawlers to index the content of websites and then use algorithms to match the keywords in a user's query with the indexed content. The search algorithm also ranks the results by relevance, taking into account factors such as the number of times the keywords appear on the page, the proximity of the keywords, and the popularity of the website.Additionally, other type of search algorithms like semantic search, image search, geospatial search, etc, which are designed to target specific data format or application areas.In summary, search algorithms work by indexing the content, matching keywords in a user's query with the indexed content, and ranking the results by relevance.What about search algorithms for mazes?There are several algorithms that can be used to find a solution to a maze, which is a problem of searching for a path through a graph. Some of the most popular algorithms for solving mazes include:Breadth-first search (BFS): This algorithm explores all the neighboring nodes at the current depth level before moving on to the next level. BFS can be used to find the shortest path in an unweighted maze.Depth-first search (DFS): This algorithm explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. DFS can be implemented recursively or with a stack.Dijkstra's algorithm: This algorithm is a modified version of BFS and is used to find the shortest path in a weighted maze.A* search algorithm: This algorithm is combination of Dijkstra's Algorithm and heuristic search, It uses an estimate of the shortest distance between the current location and the goal to guide the search, allowing it to find the shortest path more efficiently than Dijkstra's algorithm.Best-first search: Similar to A* but using a different method to estimate the distance.All of these algorithms will work correctly to find the solution of the maze, which one you should use depends on the problem you are trying to solve and the type of maze you are working with.Could you provide an example on how A* search algorithms work?Certainly! A* is a type of informed search algorithm, which means that it uses additional information, called a heuristic, to guide the search. The heuristic function estimates the cost of the cheapest path from a given node to the goal.Here's an example of how the A* algorithm works:You have a grid-based maze represented as a 2D array, where some cells are blocked and some are open. You are starting at the cell (0, 0) and the goal is to reach the cell (n-1, n-1).Create an open list and a closed list. The open list is a priority queue that stores the nodes that have been discovered but not yet expanded. The closed list is a list of nodes that have already been expanded.Add the starting cell to the open list and set its distance to the goal as zero.While the open list is not empty:Remove the cell with the lowest estimated cost from the open list and add it to the closed list.If the removed cell is the goal, you have found a solution and can stop the algorithm.Otherwise, consider each of the neighboring cells that are not blocked and not on the closed list.For each neighboring cell, calculate the distance to the goal using the heuristic function, which in this case could be the Manhattan distance,
Manhattan = |current.x - goal.x| + |current.y - goal.y|Add the neighboring cell to the open list if it's not already on it, and set its estimated cost as the sum of the distance from the start and the heuristic.A* algorithm guarantees that the path it finds is the optimal path, that is, the path with the lowest cost, because it always chooses the node with the lowest estimated total cost f(x) = g(x) + h(x), where g(x) is the actual cost from start to x, and h(x) is the estimated cost from x to the goal.It's worth to mention that in practice, the A* algorithm can run into performance issues when searching large problem spaces, one technique to mitigate that is the use of a technique called "A* search with movement pruning", which discards nodes and movements that are unlikely to be part of the solution and improves the performance.

5.3.3 Efficacy of Aerobic Training Exercise

A study from Brosseau et al. (2012) researching walking as an aerobic training and an add-on of behavioural interventions together with an educational pamphlet does not show a significant improvement in most functional outcome measures except for the level of physical activity. The same goes for the aerobic training group, with adding one educational pamphlet also unable to exhibit a significant difference compared to the control group. Most surprisingly, other outcome measures favoured the control group, which only had an educational pamphlet as the intervention. Overall, the WOMAC score exhibited a significant improvement for Group C, a self-directed control group (p<0.05). Brosseau et al. (2012) justified that it is probably due to the stress and pressure on the intervention group to be consistently involved in the interventions. At the same time, Group C can do the interventions efficiently without any pressure upon them. It is thus not aligned with a recent study from Noha et al. (2020) whereby they stated that a significant improvement in mean total WOMAC score was found in the study group (27.6±14.5) than the control group (79.8±15.9) (P= 0.000) after application of the aerobic walking program. Therefore, they concluded that aerobic walking reduces pain and improves functional ability among KOA patients. In another recent study from Sharma et al. (2015) compared to Brosseau et al. (2012), they exhibited a significant difference in VAS score at rest, during activity and also WOMAC score for the aerobic walking and strengthening group. Additionally, the mean difference in VAS during activity revealed a significant difference between groups B and A and B and C. Also, the mean difference in WOMAC scores between groups A and C was significant. The study from Brosseau et al. (2012) justified that it may be due to the development of fewer health problems and difficulty in transportation in the self-
directed group, thus explaining the improvements.

5.4 CONCLUSION

Although most treatments in exercise therapy do not show a significant improvement at the end of the trials for most outcome measures, the least, the treatments still show improvement from the baseline and a few weeks post-treatment. Furthermore, the study for OMT has shown a significant result for combining OMT with exercise therapy. From the included studies, balance training articles
unanimously proved their effectiveness in improving the functional ability of patients with KOA. While the other two, strengthening and aerobic training, do not have significant results at the end of the study. However, it can still prove the effectiveness of manual therapy and exercise therapy in managing symptoms and improving an individual's functional ability with KOA. It is due to the reason that this study does not measure the duration of effectiveness, slight improvement or any improvement at any time point will be noted and acknowledged as a success.

5.5 LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY

In all studies, the number of participants based on gender is unstable. It may or may not affects the outcome measures; however, since KOA occurred to almost anyone regardless of gender, equating the number of participants should be considered. Also, most middle-aged adults work on weekdays, thus making it harder for the studies to gather more participants from this age group. Doing the trials on weekends or post-working hours could help establish a better result for this age group. Other than that, most studies focusing on questionnaire outcome measures can be biased based on participants' perceptions, or they could be manipulating the answers. Thus, functional outcome measures should be the focus and should be done to accompany the questionnaire outcome measure. Naturally, functional outcome measures would plainly manifest an individual’s functional ability to perform ADLs.

5.6 RECOMMENDATIONS FOR FUTURE STUDIES

It is recommended for future research to explore more on other types of manual therapy as the primary treatment for managing KOA symptoms and improving individuals’' functional ability. Additionally, functional exercises as a therapy treatment could be explored further to be performed outside the study settings since KOA mainly occurs in adults aged 35 years and above. Thus, since most are in the working sector, they have limited participation in specific exercise therapy
interventions with strict procedures and protocols.

Create a 2000 words article conversational article and Rephrase this with 100% no plagiarism and unique  Typically, the next iOS minor release goes into beta within a day or two of the prior version’s main public release. So, when iOS 16.3 was released back on January 23, we expected the 16.4 beta to begin on January 24. It’s unusual, but iOS 16.4’s first beta release finally arrived on February 16, over three weeks later. Its contemporaries (iPadOS 16.4, watchOS 9.4, and macOS 13.3) also entered beta at the same time. We expect a final release of iOS 16.4 will likely come in March, possibly at Apple’s spring event.

iOS 16.4: New features
Here are some of the significant changes and additions in iOS 16.4. We will continue to update this section as more changes are discovered.

New emoji: This release adds the emoji that are part of the Unicode 15.0 standard. They include a shaking face (side to side, like “no”), several heart colors including a pink heart that was strangely absent until now, left and right pushing hands, several new animals (moose, goose, jellyfish), and a few food items and musical instruments.
Web push notifications: This release adds support for web push notifications. Web apps saved to the home screen can send system notifications through the Push API, Notifications API, and Service Workers by using the standard HTML5 Web Push API. Websites have to ask for permission just as apps do, and it has to be in response to a user action (like tapping a “subscribe” button or the like).

Home architecture upgrade: The Home architecture upgrade that was pulled from the iOS 16.2 release is back in iOS 16.4. This is separate from the upgraded Home app, which has remained.

New Podcasts app: A new Podcasts app across iPhone, iPad, and CarPlay improves the Up Next queue and adds features like episode filtering and the ability to browse by season.

5G: Standalone support for T-Mobile users to enable faster speeds where available. 
Widgets: A new Wallet widget to easily track orders. 

Mastadon support: Automatic previews for links in Messages as with Twitter.

New beta requirements: If your device is registered as a beta tester, you can open Settings > General > Software Updates and a new menu allows you to select whether you want no beta updates, Developer Beta updates (if applicable), or Public Beta updates. Also, developers will now need an authorized developer account to install updates rather than just a profile.
Apple has let loose public beta versions of iOS 16.4, iPadOS 16.4, and macOS Ventura 13.3 equipped with new emoji, web app push notifications on the mobile operating systems, and more. The release comes a day after developers were given access to the new software.

New Apple software releases are some of the first places to try the latest emoji sets before all other devices adopt them, and iOS 16.4 is no exception. You’re getting new ones from Unicode 15.0, including the “stop right there”-looking hand and a ginger root, so you can finally ask for a juice blend at the gym cafe using only emoji.

Other features it’s testing include transliteration support for South Asian languages Urdu, Punjabi, and Gujarati, 5G standalone support, notifications for web apps, tilt / orientation Apple Pencil support for hover, the return of the HomeKit architecture upgrade that Apple removed from iOS 16.2 and content previews for Mastodon links in iMessage.
In order to install the iOS 16.4 beta on your iPhone and iPad, you need to sign up with Apple to enable public beta installs via its beta software portal. The process involves you agreeing to lots of terms and conditions — beta software isn’t final and might introduce new problems or cause issues with your device — and then installing a profile on your phone that lets the update show up in Settings > General > Software Update.

However, once you’re running iOS 16.4, things should be simpler, as future beta tests will simply be linked to your Apple ID — no profile installations necessary.

imagine you have 24 questions, each with 5 different possible answers. Each answer carries a score. What is the fastest way to compute a histogram of overall scores with all the possible ways to answer these 24 questions?

**Mod 1**: If I have this histogram and I decide to change the scoring of one of the answers of one of the questions, what is the fastest way to recompute the new histogram?

**Mod 2**: How can I highlight the percentage of a bar of the histogram that is part of answering one question in a very particular way?Here are two approaches you could take to solve this problem:Approach 1:Create an array of size 625 (5^24) to store the counts of the different score combinations.For each combination of answers, compute the score by summing the scores of each individual answer and increment the count at the corresponding index in the array.To display the histogram, you can either plot the data directly or create a dictionary mapping the score to the count and use that to create the histogram.To update the histogram after changing the scoring of one answer, you would need to recalculate the scores for all combinations and update the counts in the array accordingly.Approach 2:Create a dictionary mapping each question to a list of the scores for each answer.Create a dictionary to store the counts of the different scores.For each combination of answers, compute the score by summing the scores of each individual answer and increment the count at the corresponding score in the dictionary.To display the histogram, you can create a dictionary mapping the score to the count and use that to create the histogram.To update the histogram after changing the scoring of one answer, you would only need to update the scores for that particular question and recalculate the counts for the corresponding scores.To highlight the percentage of a bar of the histogram that is part of answering one question in a particular way, you can use a stacked bar chart, where each layer represents the contribution of a particular question. Alternatively, you could use a grouped bar chart, where each group represents the contribution of a particular question.

    df['EMA'] = TA.EMA(df)#4
    df['WMA'] = TA.WMA(df)#5

    df['TEMA'] = TA.TEMA(df)#7
    df['CCI'] = TA.CCI(df)#8

    df['MACD'] = TA.MACD(df)['MACD'] - TA.MACD(df)['SIGNAL']#10
    df['PPO'] = TA.PPO(df)['PPO'] - TA.PPO(df)['SIGNAL']#11
    df['ROC'] = TA.ROC(df)#12
    df['CFI'] = TA.CFI(df)#13
    df['DMI'] = TA.DMI(df)['DI+'] - TA.DMI(df)['DI-']#14

Campaigners claim that exams favour the privileged. Evidence for this is thin. Maths problems involve neutral things like numbers and algebra; reading-comprehension tests are rarely about silverware or yachting. The bias, however, is said to be latent. Because scores are correlated with race and parental income, the exams must therefore be contaminated with racism and classism.

This confuses disparity with discrimination. Tests correctly measure educational inequality, which begins before kindergarten and grows as a result of bad policy. Just as smashing thermometers does not prevent climate change, so abandoning the measurement of educational inequality will not magic it away.

In fact, for meritocrats to abandon exams is self-defeating. Scores may be correlated with privilege, but they are probably the hardest part of an admissions application to warp with money. Children of the rich can get ample help in completing their coursework (which may receive inflated grades), hire professional writers to “edit” their essays and even spend lavishly on consultants who will help craft a delectable smorgasbord of extra-curricular activities. The best way to promote fairness would be to eliminate such a regressive pathway to admission.

In the 1920s Harvard moved to a “holistic” admissions system because its president thought it had too many Jewish students (who excelled on the standardised exam adopted in 1905). A cynical observer might conclude that universities are jettisoning quantitative measures, the lawsuit’s key evidence, to make discrimination harder to detect.

Fixing educational inequality requires more data, not less. Susan Dynarski, an economist at Harvard, makes the case that free, universal testing helps unearth promising young talent from rough backgrounds. Timely reminders about financial aid also help. For decades, elite universities have sought skin-deep diversity to paper over abysmal socioeconomic diversity, a failing that is exacerbated by legacy admissions. on:
  workflow_call:
    secrets:
      PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN:
        required: true
      TECH_PASSWORD:
        required: true
      IDAM_SECRET_PASSWORD:
        required: true

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  github-release-version:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/generate-release-candidate-version.yaml
  create-draft-github-release:
    needs: [github-release-version]
    outputs:
      release-id: ${{ fromJson(steps.create_github_release.outputs.data).id }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Create GitHub tag
        uses: octokit/request-action@v2.x
        with:
          route: POST /repos/{repo}/git/refs
          repo: ${{ github.repository }}
          ref: refs/tags/${{ needs.github-release-version.outputs.version }}
          sha: ${{ github.sha }}
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - name: Create GitHub Release
        uses: octokit/request-action@v2.x
        id: create_github_release
        with:
          route: POST /repos/{repo}/releases
          repo: ${{ github.repository }}
          tag_name: ${{ needs.github-release-version.outputs.version }}
          name: ${{ needs.github-release-version.outputs.version }}
          draft: true
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
  commit-cycle:
    needs: [ create-draft-github-release ]
    uses: ./.github/workflows/commit-cycle.yaml
    secrets:
      GPG_KEY: ${{ secrets.GPG_KEY }}
  acceptance-cycle-dev:
    needs:
    - commit-cycle
    uses: ./.github/workflows/acceptance-cycle-dev.yaml
  acceptance-cycle-pp:
    needs:
    - acceptance-cycle-dev
    uses: ./.github/workflows/acceptance-cycle-pp.yaml
  testing:
    secrets:
      PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN }}
      TECH_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TECH_PASSWORD }}
      IDAM_SECRET_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.IDAM_SECRET_PASSWORD }}
    needs:
    - acceptance-cycle-pp
    uses: ./.github/workflows/test.yaml
  upgrade-draft-github-release:
    needs: [ create-draft-github-release, acceptance-cycle-dev, acceptance-cycle-pp]
    outputs:
      prerelease: ${{ fromJson(steps.upgrade_github_release.outputs.data).prerelease }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Read pipeline properties
        run: |
          grep -v '^#' ".github/waas/pipeline.properties" | grep -v '^$' >> $GITHUB_ENV
      - name: Upgrade Github release
        uses: octokit/request-action@v2.x
        id: upgrade_github_release
        with:
          route: PATCH /repos/{repo}/releases/{release_id}
          repo: ${{ github.repository }}
          release_id: ${{ needs.create-draft-github-release.outputs.release-id }}
          draft: false
          prerelease: false
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
  downgrade-github-release:
    needs: [ create-draft-github-release, acceptance-cycle-dev, acceptance-cycle-pp ]
    if: ${{ failure() }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Downgrade Github release
        uses: octokit/request-action@v2.x
        id: update_github_prerelease
        with:
          route: PATCH /repos/{repo}/releases/{release_id}
          repo: ${{ github.repository }}
          release_id: ${{ needs.create-draft-github-release.outputs.release-id }}
          draft: false
          prerelease: true
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
  delete-github-release:
    needs: [ create-draft-github-release, acceptance-cycle-dev, acceptance-cycle-pp ]
    if: ${{ cancelled() || failure() }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Delete Github release
        uses: octokit/request-action@v2.x
        id: delete_github_release
        with:
          route: DELETE /repos/{repo}/releases/{release_id}
          repo: ${{ github.repository }}
          release_id: ${{ needs.create-draft-github-release.outputs.release-id }}
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

KEYWORDS AND PHRASES: git, version-control, git-commit, undo
PRIMARY QUESTION: I accidentally committed the wrong files to Git, but didn't push the commit to the server yet.

How do I undo those commits from the local repository?

ANSWERS TO THE PRIMARY QUESTION:
Answer 1:
Undo a commit & redo
$ git commit -m "Something terribly misguided" # (0: Your Accident)
$ git reset HEAD~                              # (1)
[ edit files as necessary ]                    # (2)
$ git add .                                    # (3)
$ git commit -c ORIG_HEAD                      # (4)
git reset is the command responsible for the undo. It will undo your last commit while leaving your working tree (the state of your files on disk) untouched. You'll need to add them again before you can commit them again).
Make corrections to working tree files.
git add anything that you want to include in your new commit.
Commit the changes, reusing the old commit message. reset copied the old head to .git/ORIG_HEAD; commit with -c ORIG_HEAD will open an editor, which initially contains the log message from the old commit and allows you to edit it. If you do not need to edit the message, you could use the -C option.
Alternatively, to edit the previous commit (or just its commit message), commit --amend will add changes within the current index to the previous commit.

To remove (not revert) a commit that has been pushed to the server, rewriting history with git push origin main --force[-with-lease] is necessary. It's almost always a bad idea to use --force; prefer --force-with-lease instead, and as noted in the git manual:

You should understand the implications of rewriting history if you [rewrite history] has already been published.

Answer 2:
Undoing a commit is a little scary if you don't know how it works. But it's actually amazingly easy if you do understand. I'll show you the 4 different ways you can undo a commit.

Say you have this, where C is your HEAD and (F) is the state of your files.

   (F)
A-B-C
    ↑
  master
Option 1: git reset --hard
You want to destroy commit C and also throw away any uncommitted changes. You do this:

git reset --hard HEAD~1
The result is:

 (F)
A-B
  ↑
master
Now B is the HEAD. Because you used --hard, your files are reset to their state at commit B.

Option 2: git reset
Maybe commit C wasn't a disaster, but just a bit off. You want to undo the commit but keep your changes for a bit of editing before you do a better commit. Starting again from here, with C as your HEAD:

   (F)
A-B-C
    ↑
  master
Do this, leaving off the --hard:

git reset HEAD~1
In this case, the result is:

   (F)
A-B-C
  ↑
master
In both cases, HEAD is just a pointer to the latest commit. When you do a git reset HEAD~1, you tell Git to move the HEAD pointer back one commit. But (unless you use --hard) you leave your files as they were. So now git status shows the changes you had checked into C. You haven't lost a thing!

Option 3: git reset --soft
For the lightest touch, you can even undo your commit but leave your files and your index:

git reset --soft HEAD~1
This not only leaves your files alone, it even leaves your index alone. When you do git status, you'll see that the same files are in the index as before. In fact, right after this command, you could do git commit and you'd be redoing the same commit you just had.

Option 4: you did git reset --hard and need to get that code back
One more thing: Suppose you destroy a commit as in the first example, but then discover you needed it after all? Tough luck, right?

Nope, there's still a way to get it back. Type this

git reflog
and you'll see a list of (partial) commit shas (that is, hashes) that you've moved around in. Find the commit you destroyed, and do this:

git checkout -b someNewBranchName shaYouDestroyed
You've now resurrected that commit. Commits don't actually get destroyed in Git for some 90 days, so you can usually go back and rescue one you didn't mean to get rid of.

She then continued to ask the participants to recall a specific experience and context where they had to use communication strategies. Scott concludes that the results of the experiment indicate that young black women perceive their communication strategies to be a necessary life skill in order to succeed in such environments as predominant white communities and the importance of being aware of historical perceptions of Black Women and providing “teach- able moments” to those in predominantly white communities. In some reinforcement learning algorithms, such as Deep Q-Networks (DQN), a neural network is used to approximate the Q-function in the MDP.
The Q-function (also known as the action-value function) is a function that maps a state-action pair to an expected cumulative reward. It represents the expected sum of rewards that can be obtained by taking a particular action in a particular state and then following the optimal policy thereafter.
In the DQN algorithm, a neural network is used to approximate the Q-function. The neural network takes in the state as input and outputs the expected value for each possible action in that state. During training, the network is trained to minimize the difference between its predicted Q-values and the true Q-values obtained through a Bellman equation update.
The neural network replaces the table used to store Q-values in traditional Q-learning algorithms. By approximating the Q-function using a neural network, the DQN algorithm can handle problems with high-dimensional state spaces, making it applicable to a wide range of real-world problems.
Overall, the neural network in the DQN algorithm is used to approximate the Q-function, allowing the agent to learn an optimal policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward.

## Background
From a company for sports statistics, we obtained data and profile photos from all soccer players (N = 2053) playing in the first male divisions of England, Germany, France, and Spain in the 2012-2013 season and all referees (N = 3147) that these players played under in their professional career. We created a dataset of player referee dyads including the number of matches players and referees encountered each other and our dependent variable, the number of red cards given to a player by a particular referee throughout all matches the two encountered each other.
Player photos were available from the source for 1586 out of 2053 players. Players' skin tone was coded by two independent raters blind to the research question who, based on their profile photo, categorized players on a 5-point scale ranging from very light skin to very dark skin with neither dark nor light skin as the center value. 
Additionally, implicit bias scores for each referee country were calculated using a race implicit association test (IAT), with higher values corresponding to faster white | good, black | bad associations. Explicit bias scores for each referee country were calculated using a racial thermometer task, with higher values corresponding to greater feelings of warmth toward whites versus blacks. Both these measures were created by aggregating data from many online users in referee countries taking these tests on.
In all, the dataset has a total of 146028 dyads of players and referees. A detailed description of all variables in the dataset can be seen in the list below.

Variables:
playerShort - short player ID
player - player name
club - player club
leagueCountry - country of player club (England, Germany, France, and Spain)
birthday - player birthday
height - player height (in cm)
weight - player weight (in kg)
position  - detailed player position 
games - number of games in the player-referee dyad
victories  - victories in the player-referee dyad
ties - ties in the player-referee dyad
defeats - losses in the player-referee dyad
goals - goals scored by a player in the player-referee dyad
yellowCards - number of yellow cards player received from referee
yellowReds - number of yellow-red cards player received from referee
redCards - number of red cards player received from referee
photoID - ID of player photo (if available)

rater1 - skin rating of photo by rater 1 (5-point scale ranging from very light skin to very dark skin )
rater2 - skin rating of photo by rater 2 (5-point scale ranging from very light skin to very dark skin )
refNum - unique referee ID number (referee name removed for anonymizing purposes)
refCountry - unique referee country ID number (country name removed for anonymizing purposes)
meanIAT - mean implicit bias score (using the race IAT) for referee country, higher values correspond to faster white | good, black | bad associations 
nIAT - sample size for race IAT in that particular country
seIAT - standard error for mean estimate of race IAT       
meanExp - mean explicit bias score (using a racial thermometer task) for referee country, higher values correspond to greater feelings of warmth toward whites versus blacks
nExp - sample size for explicit bias in that particular country
seExp - standard error for mean estimate of explicit bias measure

We want to conduct an analysis for the above dataset by answering the question of  whether soccer players with dark skin tone are more likely than those with light skin tone to receive red cards from referees.

Question title: Why is __aexit__ not fully executed when it has await inside?

Question body: This is the simplified version of my code:

main is a coroutine which stops after the second iteration.
get_numbers is an async generator which yields numbers but within an async context manager.

import asyncio


class MyContextManager:
    async def __aenter__(self):
        print("Enter to the Context Manager...")
        return self

    async def __aexit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, exc_tb):
        print(exc_type)
        print("Exit from the Context Manager...")
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        print("This line is not executed")  # <-------------------
        await asyncio.sleep(1)


async def get_numbers():
    async with MyContextManager():
        for i in range(30):
            yield i


async def main():
    async for i in get_numbers():
        print(i)
        if i == 1:
            break


asyncio.run(main())
And the output is:

Enter to the Context Manager...
0
1
<class 'asyncio.exceptions.CancelledError'>
Exit from the Context Manager...
I have two questions actually:

1. From my understanding, AsyncIO schedules a Task to be called soon in the next cycle of the event loop and gives __aexit__ a chance to execute. But the line print("This line is not executed") is not executed. Why is that? Is it correct to assume that if we have an await statement inside the __aexit__, the code after that line is not going to execute at all and we shouldn't rely on that for cleaning?

2. Output of the help() on async generators shows that:
 |  aclose(...)
 |      aclose() -> raise GeneratorExit inside generator.
so why I get <class 'asyncio.exceptions.CancelledError'> exception inside the __aexit__ ?

* I'm using Python 3.10.4In the example you've provided, the main coroutine is breaking out of the loop inside the async generator after the second iteration. This causes the generator to raise the asyncio.exceptions.CancelledError exception, which is caught by the __aexit__ method of the context manager. The __aexit__ method is then scheduled to run on the next cycle of the event loop, but since the main coroutine has already stopped executing, it doesn't get a chance to execute the line "This line is not executed".The aclose method is used to raise the GeneratorExit exception inside the generator, which can be caught and handled by the generator's __aexit__ method. In this example, the main coroutine is breaking out of the loop and the generator is raised CancelledError instead of GeneratorExit
And since the CancelledError exception was raised by the generator before the aclose method was called, the __aexit__ method of the context manager is handling the CancelledError instead of the GeneratorExit.
And it's correct to assume that if we have an await statement inside the __aexit__, the code after that line is not going to execute if any exceptions was raised before await statement. But __aexit__ will always run regardless of exception or no exception

Jeff Bezos: la historia de éxito del fundador de Amazon
Jeff Bezos es uno de los empresarios más exitosos de nuestro tiempo, reconocido por su liderazgo en la transformación del sector del comercio minorista en línea. Nacido el 12 de enero de 1964 en Albuquerque, Nuevo México, desde pequeño mostró un gran interés por la tecnología y la innovación.

Después de graduarse en la Universidad de Princeton en 1986, Bezos trabajó en varias empresas tecnológicas antes de perseguir su sueño de abrir una librería en línea en 1994. Con una inversión inicial de 300,000 dólares, Bezos fundó Amazon.com en Seattle, Washington.

A pesar de las dificultades iniciales y el escepticismo de los inversores, Amazon creció rápidamente y en 1997, la empresa salió a bolsa y el precio de sus acciones se disparó, convirtiendo a Bezos en multimillonario. Bajo su liderazgo, Amazon amplió su oferta de productos y servicios para incluir desde electrónica y juguetes hasta ropa y muebles, y lanzó Amazon Web Services, una plataforma de computación en nube líder en la industria tecnológica.

La filosofía empresarial de Bezos se basa en la innovación constante, la experimentación y la creación de una cultura empresarial que valore la creatividad y el espíritu emprendedor. También cree en poner al cliente en primer lugar y en pensar a largo plazo sin temer tomar riesgos.

Fuera de Amazon, Bezos es conocido por su perfil bajo y sus esfuerzos filantrópicos. En 2018, lanzó el Fondo Day One para ayudar a las familias sin hogar y crear centros preescolares de alta calidad en comunidades de bajos ingresos.

Aunque ha sido criticado por el trato a los empleados de Amazon y el impacto de la empresa en las pequeñas empresas, Jeff Bezos ha dejado una huella indeleble en el mundo empresarial. Su visión e innovación han transformado la forma de comprar y allanado el camino para el futuro del comercio minorista. Su filosofía empresarial y valores personales también han contribuido a su éxito, lo que lo convierte en un modelo a seguir para muchos emprendedores.

Bukan karena ia hanya bercerita tentang kalangan miskin, Putu Wijaya tak tertarik untuk berbicara tentang lapisan-lapisan sosial. Teater Mandiri adalah “teater miskin” karena ia, sebagaimana yang kemudian dijadikan semboyan kreatif Putu Wijaya, ”bertolak dari yang ada”. 

Saya ingat bagaimana pada tahun 1971, Putu Wijaya memulainya. Ia bekerja sebagai salah satu redaktur majalah Tempo, yang berkantor di sebuah gedung tua bertingkat dua dengan lantai yang goyang di Jalan Senen Raya 83, Jakarta. Siang hari ia akan bertugas sebagai wartawan. Malam hari, ketika kantor sepi, ia akan menggunakan ruangan yang terbatas dan sudah aus itu untuk latihan teater. Dan ia akan mengajak siapa saja: seorang tukang kayu muda yang di waktu siang memperbaiki bangunan kantor, seorang gelandangan tua yang tiap malam istirahat di pojok jalan itu, seorang calon fotografer yang gagap. Ia tak menuntut mereka untuk berakting dan mengucapkan dialog yang cakap. Ia membuat mereka jadi bagian teater sebagai peristiwa, bukan hanya cerita.

Dari sini memang kemudian berkembang gaya Putu Wijaya: sebuah teater yang dibangun dari dialektik antara ”peristiwa” dan ”cerita”, antara kehadiran aktor dan orang-orang yang hanya bagian komposisi panggung, antara kata sebagai alat komunikasi dan kata sebagai benda tersendiri. Juga teater yang hidup dari tarik-menarik antara patos dan humor, antara suasana yang terbangun utuh dan disintegrasi yang segera mengubah keutuhan itu.

Orang memang bisa ragu, apa sebenarnya yang dibangun (dan dibangunkan) oleh teater Putu Wijaya. Keraguan ini bisa dimengerti. Indonesia didirikan dan diatur oleh sebuah lapisan elite yang berpandangan bahwa yang dibangun haruslah sebuah “bangunan”, sebuah tata, bahkan tata yang permanen. Elite itu juga menganggap bahwa kebangunan adalah kebangkitan dari ketidaksadaran. Ketika Putu Wijaya memilih kata “teror” dalam hubungan dengan karya kreatifnya, bagi saya ia menampik pandangan seperti itu. Pentasnya menunjukkan bahwa pada tiap tata selalu tersembunyi chaos, dan pada tiap ucapan yang transparan selalu tersembunyi ketidaksadaran.

Sartre pernah mengatakan, salah satu motif menciptakan seni adalah “memperkenalkan tata di mana ia semula tak ada, memasangkan kesatuan pikiran dalam keragaman hal-ihwal”. Saya kira ia salah. Ia mungkin berpikir tentang keindahan dalam pengertian klasik, di mana tata amat penting. Bagi saya Teater Mandiri justru menunjukkan bahwa di sebuah negeri di mana tradisi dan anti tradisi berbenturan (tapi juga sering berkelindan), bukan pengertian klasik itu yang berlaku.

Pernah pula Sartre mengatakan, seraya meremehkan puisi, bahwa ”kata adalah aksi”. Prosa, menurut Sartre, “terlibat” dalam pembebasan manusia karena memakai kata sebagai alat mengkomunikasikan ide, sedangkan puisi tidak. Namun, di sini pun Sartre salah. Ia tak melihat, prosa dan puisi bisa bertaut—dan itu bertaut dengan hidup dalam teater Putu Wijaya. Puisi dalam teater ini muncul ketika keharusan berkomunikasi dipatahkan. Sebagaimana dalam puisi, dalam sajak Chairil Anwar apalagi dalam sajak Sutardji Calzoum Bachri, yang hadir dalam pentas Teater Mandiri adalah imaji-imaji, bayangan dan bunyi, bukan pesan, apalagi khotbah. Hal ini penting, di zaman ketika komunikasi hanya dibangun oleh pesan verbal yang itu-itu saja, yang tak lagi akrab dengan diri, hanya hasil kesepakatan orang lain yang kian asing.

Sartre kemudian menyadari ia salah. Sejak 1960-an, ia mengakui bahwa bahasa bukan alat yang siap. Bahasa tak bisa mengungkapkan apa yang ada di bawah sadar, tak bisa mengartikulasikan hidup yang dijalani, le vecu. Ia tentu belum pernah menyaksikan pentas Teater Mandiri, tapi ia pasti melihat bahwa pelbagai ekspresi teater dan kesusastraan punya daya “teror” ketika, seperti Teater Mandiri, menunjukkan hal-hal yang tak terkomunikasikan dalam hidup. 

Sebab yang tak terkatakan juga bagian dari “yang ada”. Dari sana kreativitas yang sejati bertolak.

## Background
From a company for sports statistics, we obtained data and profile photos from all soccer players (N = 2053) playing in the first male divisions of England, Germany, France, and Spain in the 2012-2013 season and all referees (N = 3147) that these players played under in their professional career. We created a dataset of player\'96referee dyads including the number of matches players and referees encountered each other and our dependent variable, the number of red cards given to a player by a particular referee throughout all matches the two encountered each other.
Player photos were available from the source for 1586 out of 2053 players. Players' skin tone was coded by two independent raters blind to the research question who, based on their profile photo, categorized players on a 5-point scale ranging from very light skin to very dark skin with neither dark nor light skin as the center value. 
Additionally, implicit bias scores for each referee country were calculated using a race implicit association test (IAT), with higher values corresponding to faster white | good, black | bad associations. Explicit bias scores for each referee country were calculated using a racial thermometer task, with higher values corresponding to greater feelings of warmth toward whites versus blacks. Both these measures were created by aggregating data from many online users in referee countries taking these tests on.
In all, the dataset has a total of 146028 dyads of players and referees. A detailed description of all variables in the dataset can be seen in the list below.

Variables:
playerShort - short player ID
player - player name
club - player club
leagueCountry - country of player club (England, Germany, France, and Spain)
birthday - player birthday
height - player height (in cm)
weight - player weight (in kg)
position  - detailed player position 
games - number of games in the player-referee dyad
victories  - victories in the player-referee dyad
ties - ties in the player-referee dyad
defeats - losses in the player-referee dyad
goals - goals scored by a player in the player-referee dyad
yellowCards - number of yellow cards player received from referee
yellowReds - number of yellow-red cards player received from referee
redCards - number of red cards player received from referee
photoID - ID of player photo (if available)

rater1 - skin rating of photo by rater 1 (5-point scale ranging from very light skin to very dark skin )
rater2 - skin rating of photo by rater 2 (5-point scale ranging from very light skin to very dark skin )
refNum - unique referee ID number (referee name removed for anonymizing purposes)
refCountry - unique referee country ID number (country name removed for anonymizing purposes)
meanIAT - mean implicit bias score (using the race IAT) for referee country, higher values correspond to faster white | good, black | bad associations 
nIAT - sample size for race IAT in that particular country
seIAT - standard error for mean estimate of race IAT       
meanExp - mean explicit bias score (using a racial thermometer task) for referee country, higher values correspond to greater feelings of warmth toward whites versus blacks
nExp - sample size for explicit bias in that particular country
seExp - standard error for mean estimate of explicit bias measure

We want to conduct an analysis for the above dataset by answering the question of  whether soccer players with dark skin tone are more likely than those with light skin tone to receive red cards from referees.

write an essay on spontaneity in public speaking in 1000 wordsSpontaneity in public speaking is the ability to speak in an unplanned, unscripted, and improvised manner. It is the ability to think on your feet, to react and respond to your audience and the situation in a way that is authentic and engaging.Spontaneity can be a powerful tool for public speakers. It allows you to be more authentic, to connect with your audience in a more meaningful way, and to improvise and adapt to the needs of the moment. It can also add energy, enthusiasm, and excitement to your presentation, making it more engaging and memorable for your audience.However, spontaneity in public speaking also requires a certain level of skill and preparation. It is not simply about winging it or improvising without any thought or planning. Rather, it is about being prepared and confident enough to respond and adapt to the needs of the moment, while still staying true to your message and purpose.One way to cultivate spontaneity in public speaking is to practice improvisation and impromptu speaking. This can involve giving impromptu speeches, taking part in improvisation games and exercises, or simply allowing yourself to be more spontaneous in your everyday interactions. By practicing improv and impromptu speaking, you can develop your ability to think on your feet, to come up with ideas and responses quickly, and to adapt to changing circumstances.Another way to cultivate spontaneity in public speaking is to be well-prepared and knowledgeable about your topic. While spontaneity is about being unplanned and improvised, it does not mean that you should be unprepared or ignorant about your subject matter. In fact, being well-prepared and knowledgeable about your topic can give you the confidence and foundation you need to be spontaneous and adaptable in your presentation.For example, if you are giving a presentation on a particular subject, you should make sure to research and understand the topic thoroughly. This will give you the knowledge and background you need to speak confidently and authentically about the subject. It will also give you a foundation of information that you can draw upon when improvising and adapting to the needs of the moment.Another key to cultivating spontaneity in public speaking is to be authentic and genuine. This means being yourself and speaking from the heart, rather than trying to be someone you are not or delivering a rehearsed and scripted presentation. When you are authentic and genuine in your public speaking, it allows you to connect with your audience in a more meaningful and authentic way. It also allows you to be more spontaneous and adaptable, as you are not tied to a script or a predetermined way of speaking.Finally, it is important to remember that spontaneity in public speaking is not about being perfect or flawless. It is about being authentic, genuine, and adaptable in the moment. It is about responding and reacting to your audience and the situation in a way that is natural and engaging. By cultivating spontaneity in your public speaking, you can become a more confident, authentic, and effective speaker, and better connect with your audience.
